prose.def: An essentially untranslatable Greek particle marking a clause as part of a pair (usually answered by δέ), or standing alone for emphasis or concession.
senseLabels: sets up a contrast / correlative pair
prose.article: μέν is one of Greek's little signpost words: it marks the clause it sits in as the first half of a pairing, typically answered later by δέ ("this one... but that one"). It is so dependent on context that it is genuinely untranslatable — in the Byzantine New Testament it absorbs into the surrounding phrasing 136 of its 194 times, with no English word of its own. When it does surface, translators render it all sorts of ways ("is," "indeed," "one," "they," "with," "there"), and notably the BSB agrees 0% of the time on the "indeed" renderings, showing how loosely it maps to English. Moulton-Milligan even cites an everyday papyrus letter (BGU II.423) where μέν stands alone in a greeting, "first of all I pray that you are well."
prose.caution: The measured "senses" here are mostly translation artifacts of how μέν gets folded into English clauses, not distinct meanings, and the lexica agree it is essentially untranslatable, so treat the sense labels loosely.

prose.def: A strong emphatic particle meaning 'nay rather' or 'indeed,' used to correct, intensify, or redirect what was just said.

prose.article: μέντοι is a little Greek particle that signals contrast or qualification — roughly "however," "yet," or "nevertheless." It appears only 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 4 books, and the lexicons agree it originally was a strengthened form of μέν, sometimes carrying an emphatic "indeed, really" sense. Everyday papyri show it working exactly this way: one second-century letter uses it in the phrase "do not be disturbed, however" (μηδὲν μέντοι θορυβηθῇς), confirming it as common conversational Koine. Note that in James 2:8 it pairs with εἰ to mean something like "if indeed."

prose.def: To stay in a place, continue in a state or relationship, or wait/endure over time; in John especially, to dwell mutually in intimate union.
prose.article: At its core μένω means to stay put — whether physically lodging somewhere, holding to a state or relationship, or lasting through time. prose.def: To divide something into parts, distribute or apportion shares among people, or (of a person or community) to be split apart or inwardly distracted.
prose.article: μερίζω basically means to split something up—either literally cutting it into portions or distributing and assigning shares to people. In the Byzantine New Testament its measured uses lean toward conflict imagery, with 7 of 10 clear cases describing a kingdom or house "divided against itself" or "divided against" something, while the rest cover ordinary division or apportioning. The everyday Koine papyri show the practical financial side vividly: one document describes a mother who "bestowed" four arourae of land each upon her children, and another mentions land "assigned" instead of a subvention. In the Septuagint it most often translates the Hebrew חָלַק, the standard word for dividing or apportioning.

The everyday papyri capture this vividly: a wife writes to her husband that, lying awake night and day, she has "one care" (μίαν μέριμναν) for his safety, showing the word's pull toward genuine fear for a loved one.

prose.def: A negative particle meaning 'not' or 'do not,' functioning in commands, wishes, conditions, and purpose clauses rather than straightforward factual denials.
prose.article: μή is Greek's qualified or subjective negative, the partner to οὐ: where οὐ flatly denies a fact, μή denies in the realm of will, thought, and possibility — so it dominates commands, conditions, and purpose clauses. Across 1,029 Byzantine occurrences it is rendered most simply as 'not' (240×, 40%) and 'do not' (119×, 20%), but it appears in dozens of small combinations and is absorbed into English phrasing 426 times with no word of its own. In the Septuagint it translates several Hebrew negatives, most often לֹא ('not', 632×) and אַל (the prohibitive 'do not', 556×), neatly matching its command-and-prohibition role.
prose.caution: The many one- and two-word renderings reflect English grammar packaging the same particle rather than distinct meanings, so the sense list should be read as patterns of usage, not separate definitions.

prose.def: A written variant of the two separate words μή τις, used in indirect questions meaning 'whether anyone'; absent from the Byzantine NT and not a distinct lexical unit.
prose.article: μήτις is really the negative particle μή joined to the indefinite pronoun τὶς, written as one word in some older printed texts but treated as two words (μή τις) by modern editors. It functions in questions, where it signals "whether anyone" or expects the answer "no," sometimes carried only by the questioning tone of the sentence rather than a separate translated word. A nice everyday example survives in a papyrus from 13 B.C. (BGU IV.1141), where a writer says he asks the doorkeeper daily "whether anyone has slept outside" — showing the same construction in ordinary indirect questions.
prose.caution: The evidence digest records zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament and notes that grammarians treat it as the two separate words μή τις, so its status as a distinct "word" is disputed.

prose.def: The neuter of μικρός, used adverbially or substantively to mean a little, a little while (especially of time), or small/low in size, age, or rank.
prose.article: μικρόν is the neuter singular of the adjective μικρός ("small, little"), used on its own as a noun or adverb. Its range is wide: it can mean little in size or quantity (Matthew 13:32; Luke 12:32), young in age (Mark 15:40), low in rank or importance (Matthew 10:42; 11:11), or a short space of time. That last use is the most common in the Gospels — μικρόν standing for "a little while" (John 13:33), with μετὰ μικρόν meaning "after a little while" (Matthew 26:73), and it can simply work as the adverb "a little" (Matthew 26:39).

prose.def: Small in size, quantity, rank, or duration; used of persons, things, and spans of time, including comparative forms meaning 'least.'
prose.article: μικρός is a basic, everyday Greek word for "small" that stretches across several dimensions: physical size, quantity, social rank, and even time. In the New Testament it appears 45 times, most often meaning simply "little" (15×), but it also marks a short span as "a little while" (7×) and can describe someone of low standing—the "little ones" or the "least." In the Septuagint it shows up 133 times, mostly rendering the Hebrew קָטָן (small, 53×) and מְעָט (few, 34×); interestingly, papyri suggest it was sometimes used to mean "junior" by age rather than short in stature, though the evidence there is mixed.

prose.article: Miletus is a proper name for a maritime city in the region of Caria, on the coast of the Roman province of Asia. It appears 3 times in the New Testament, always rendered "Miletus," twice in Acts 20 (verses 15 and 17) and once in 2 Timothy 4:20. Interestingly, the name also shows up once in the Septuagint, where it stands in for the Hebrew word חֶלְבּוֹן (Helbon), suggesting it was occasionally used to translate other place-related terms.
prose.caution: This is a proper place name with only 3 New Testament occurrences and uncertain origin, so the lone Septuagint match to a different Hebrew word should be treated carefully.

prose.def: A Roman mile, a unit of distance equal to about 1,000 paces or eight stades—slightly less than a modern mile.
prose.article: μίλιον is a measure of distance: the Roman mile, reckoned at 1,000 paces, eight stades, or roughly 1,478 meters. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Jesus's words about going an extra mile (Matthew 5:41), and every translation surveyed renders it simply as "mile." The word is itself a borrowing from Latin (milia passuum), and the papyri confirm its everyday use—one document describes two villages as being "less than a mile apart."
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its range cannot be measured across varied contexts.
